question: Will the Kennedy Center's main building be open to the general public on October 2, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Status quo is closed: fenced, locked, staff told not to report, since Sept 16. The party controlling the doors wants the building shut for two years and moved on Sept 19 to dissolve the injunction blocking that; Trump has publicly threatened demolition and conditioned reopening on the naming dispute. The stated safety grounds (Grand Foyer ceiling collapse, roof terrace canopy, soffit panels, electrical) are the kind that take months, and the week-to-week reevaluation is a ratchet Beatty's own lawyers called 'a recipe for extending their shutdown forever.' There is no forcing event: the 2026-27 calendar is unfilled, the NSO has relocated to six other venues, and the Sept 18 layoffs gutted marketing/sales. The realistic YES route is Judge Cooper reading the Sept 23 status report as pretext and ordering reopening, with the administration physically admitting the public by Oct 2 — he has ruled against them four times, but he also declined emergency relief and allowed the closure plus 'emergency repairs' to continue. I price that chain at roughly 12-18% for an order and about half of that converting to actual public entry inside the window, plus ~2-3% for a voluntary partial reopening of safe areas (which would count). Thin, one-directional evidence on the operational side keeps me near the conditional base rate.

STATUS-QUO OUTCOME: main building physically closed. Doors locked 6pm Tue Sept 15; closure effective Wed Sept 16; bike racks stacked at entrances and new fencing erected; lights off; staff emailed that nonessential employees should not report. That is the condition in force at Now, day 6 of the closure.

EVIDENCE — mechanism and timeline:
- Sept 15, 2026: board of trustees (Trump-chaired) voted to close the center immediately for repairs, hours after Judge Cooper barred re-inscribing Trump's name on the facade. CFO Donna Arduin Kauranen resigned same day. (Wikipedia/Kennedy Center; NBC News, Sept 15-16)
- Sept 16: Trump and Bill Pulte photographed on Air Force One with a board reading 'Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED'; Trump said the venue could 'end up being ripped down' absent recognition, and that he would scrap renovations without his name on the facade. (CNN/WaPo, Sept 16)
- Sept 17: Exec Dir Matt Floca declaration — closure of the main building for seven days 'unless extended,' citing 'acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration'; he will assess severely deteriorated portions and 'reevaluate the need for continued closure on a weekly basis,' opening areas found safe. Triggers named: summer engineering assessment of the roof terrace canopy; water leak from the Sept 4 DC storm collapsing ~60 ft of Grand Foyer ceiling plaster; staff email also flags soffit panels and electrical infrastructure. Seventh day falls Sept 23. (The Hill / Denver Gazette / ABC, Sept 17)
- Sept 17: Cooper DENIED Beatty's request for an emergency hearing on the closure; ordered defendants to file a detailed status report with a sworn declaration on the 'temporary closure' and emergency repairs by Sept 23; ordered discovery into board actions re demolition; required 30 days' notice before demolition or major physical alteration; required notice of any reversal of the no-demolition position. (Axios / Washingtonian / The Hill, Sept 17)
- Sept 18: second layoff round — ~14 staff including top spokesperson Roma Daravi, board-relations head Joe LaFauci, and IT / communications / marketing-and-sales personnel. (Washington Post, Sept 18)
- Sept 19 (Friday night): DOJ filed a motion asking Cooper to RESCIND/dissolve the May 29 preliminary injunction that blocked the two-year closure, arguing the board now has a complete plan including continuing programming at other sites while the main building is shuttered. Ruling timing not announced. (Washington Times, Sept 19)
- Sept 18 and Sept 21: protests of 1,000+ organized by Hands Off the Arts; human chain around the building; Gay Men's Chorus of Washington performed outside. (GW Hatchet, Sept 21; WaPo)
- Prior litigation posture: May 29, 2026 Cooper order restored the original name, required the extended renovation plan be reconsidered, temporarily BLOCKED the proposed two-year shutdown, and restored ex officio trustee voting rights. Center's June 11 notice of appeal and stay request denied by Cooper June 12; D.C. Circuit denied both an emergency administrative stay and a stay pending appeal. So an injunction barring a prolonged shutdown is in force at Now. DOJ's position: 'No part of the Court's preliminary injunction order forbids a temporary closure like this one.' Beatty's position: the temporary framing is 'a plain pretext,' 'a recipe for Defendants extending their shutdown forever'; her filings cite a witness account of a forklift striking building pillars and same-day fencing.
- Programming: the 2026-27 main-building calendar is described as unfilled. The National Symphony Orchestra moved its entire 2026-27 season off-site — 24 concerts at Lisner, 13 at Strathmore, 9 at Schlesinger, 8 at GMU Center for the Arts, 2 each at Clarice Smith and Lincoln Theatre; NSO October dates are Oct 8-9 and Oct 22-23, both off-site. (WTOP / AP, Aug 2026)
- The REACH annex remains open and operating: free performances listed Sept 23-24, Dolly Parton celebration Sept 25. Under the criteria this is outside the resolving structure.
- Finances: management told the board the institution was near bankruptcy and could not support payroll obligations or routine maintenance contracts within weeks; board resolutions called the building 'unsafe for continued occupancy,' which Beatty says the board's own construction consultants never stated. (WaPo, Sept 14-15; NPR/Houston Public Media, Sept 14)

calls.reasoning: Main building closed to public since Sept 16 under a sworn 'seven days, unless extended' safety declaration with weekly reevaluation; Oct 2 is ~16 days into that closure. Every actor controlling the reopening decision wants the building shut: board voted 23-3 for a two-year closure, Trump declared closure immediate, DOJ is moving to dissolve the May injunction to permit it, and layoffs of the staff who would run public access began Sept 18. Resident companies (NSO, WNO) have relocated their entire 2026-27 seasons, so there is no programming pulling the doors open. Real structural hazards (Sept 4 Grand Foyer plaster collapse, roof-terrace canopy assessment) give an extendable, court-resistant rationale. YES requires either a voluntary partial reopening to avoid contempt or a fast Cooper order after the Sept 23 status report plus compliance within nine days; Cooper already denied an emergency hearing and his own injunction contemplated a properly-taken new closure vote. Thin spot: no credible reporting yet on whether the seven days was formally extended.

STATUS QUO OUTCOME: main building physically closed to the public (black fencing, doors barricaded, staff entering via parking garage) since Wed Sept 16, 2026; REACH campus open; that is the state the world is in absent a change.

EVIDENCE
- Sept 15, 2026: board of trustees (Trump as chair) voted 23-3 to close the main building 'forthwith' for a ~2-year, $285M renovation; vote came roughly an hour after Judge Cooper blocked adding Trump's name/'Trump Plaza' to the building. (Variety, CNBC, Sept 15-17)
- Sept 16: main building closed to the public without notice; fencing installed; CNN observed no closure signage, digital boards still advertising shows, employees entering through the garage. (CNN Sept 16)
- Sept 17: Executive Director Matt Floca's sworn declaration states he independently cut off public access over 'acute risks to public safety'; closure 'will last for seven days, unless extended,' with need for continued closure 'reevaluate[d]... on a weekly basis,' and that he would try to open areas deemed safe. Seven days from Sept 16 = ~Sept 23. (The Hill, Washington Examiner, Denver Gazette, Sept 17)
- Physical basis cited: Sept 4 DC storm; a large water-damaged plaster section (~1.5 m) fell ~60 ft to the Grand Foyer floor, no injuries; summer engineering assessment of the roof terrace canopy; a recent water leak; staff email also flagged soffit panels and electrical infrastructure. (The Hill, ABC, Estadao Sept 20)
- Floca to staff: the closure 'is not a decision to effectuate the Board's separate vote to close the building for renovation... pending the Court's ruling on that vote.' DOJ (Brantley Mayers): 'No part of the Court's preliminary injunction order forbids a temporary closure like this one,' and defendants 'intend to move for dissolution of the preliminary injunction to allow for the closure.' (The Hill, Sept 17)
- May 2026 preliminary injunction (Judge Christopher Cooper, D.D.C.): barred closure and ordered Trump's name removed; expressly stated it 'will not prevent the Center from moving forward with the capital repair work it has planned' and would not 'categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations... in a prudent fashion'; remains in force 'until the Board approves any closure consistent with' the ruling 'and the Court issues a further Order dissolving or modifying' it. Cooper had also earlier ordered the administration to give board members renovation plans before any closure vote. (NBC News; CourtListener docket 287972; AOL)
- Sept 17 rulings: Cooper DENIED Beatty's emergency hearing request; ordered a detailed status report with sworn declaration on the temporary closure and emergency repairs due Sept 23; required 30 days' notice before demolition or major physical alteration; allowed Beatty additional discovery; said he would review the status report before deciding on further hearings. (Axios, CNBC, The Hill, Sept 17)
- Beatty's position: closure is 'unexplained and unlawful' and 'a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently'; a staff member was turned away by guards who said the building was closed and interior construction was beginning. Beatty has also publicly asserted the center is still (legally) open. (Washington Examiner, CNBC, KVIA)
- Trump (Truth Social): closure immediate, but 'Renovation and Reconstruction... cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name'; if that ruling is negative and not overturned by the Supreme Court, the reconstruction 'will not take place.'
- Sept 18: more than a dozen employees laid off, including top spokesperson Roma Daravi, board-relations head Joe LaFauci, and marketing leadership, 'as closure continues'; an earlier layoff round occurred in March 2026. (Washington Post / Spokesman Sept 18)
- Sept 18: 'Hands Off the Arts' protest of thousands outside the closed building. (JoeMyGod)
- Programming context: National Symphony Orchestra announced Aug 18 it will play its entire 2026-27 classical season (64 concerts) at six non-Kennedy-Center venues, opening Sept 26; Washington National Opera left in January for Lisner Auditorium; CNN reported in Feb 2026 that leadership had been unable to sign enough acts for a 2026-27 season and no performances were announced after July 4, 2026. Center said Honors and Mark Twain Prize would continue, possibly offsite; education programming continues at the REACH. (WTOP, SFCV, Symphony.org, Al Jazeera)
- Finances: $257M congressional appropriation (July 2025) for repairs; board claimed near-bankruptcy on Sept 14; donor and ticket support collapsed after the 2025 takeover (a typical fall-2025 production sold ~57% of tickets vs ~93% in fall 2024).
- Manipulation-signal note: much of the available reporting is openly partisan on both sides (administration statements vs. plaintiff statements); the 'pretext' characterization is litigation argument, and the 'life-safety' characterization is a sworn but interested declaration.

calls.reasoning: Status quo is closed-and-fenced since Sept 16, and the status quo is the heavy favorite over a 10-day horizon. Reference class: 'temporary' safety closures where the controlling authority has separately voted for a multi-year shutdown reopen within two weeks maybe ~15% of the time unconditionally; here every conditioning variable points lower. Floca, who authored the seven-day declaration, publicly claimed the two-year closure as his own idea (CNN, Apr 22) and built in weekly-extension language; 14+ senior staff were laid off Sept 18; the NSO relocated its whole 2026-27 season (incl. October dates) to six other venues and the board never approved its Oct 1 FY budget - so there is no programming, staffing, or institutional reason to admit the public on Oct 2. The one real YES path is judicial: Cooper's May 29 preliminary injunction arguably bars this shutdown. But offered an emergency order on Sept 16, he declined to compel reopening, opting for a Sept 23 status report and discovery through Oct 9, and his Sept 17 order expressly does not require immediate reopening - judges rarely order the public into a building against a sworn imminent-life-safety declaration, and DOJ would seek a stay. Counterweight kept in the number: the YES bar is extremely low (any public entry, any purpose, any moment on Oct 2), and defendants have a contempt-mitigation incentive to stage a token Grand Foyer reopening. I price court-compelled access on Oct 2 at ~5% and a voluntary partial reopening at ~4%. No market matches this contract (Polymarket books are on demolition announcements, $183-247 volume); kennedy-center.org returned 403, so I could not verify listed hours directly - the criteria make physical access controlling anyway.

STATUS-QUO OUTCOME: main building closed to public entry. It was locked at 6pm Tue Sept 15 / closed Wed Sept 16, 2026; bike racks then construction fencing were placed at entrances; new fencing appeared Sept 16 (WaPo, Sept 18). The Sept 18 protest could not complete a human chain because portions were fenced off, and demonstrators stood in front of a 'fenced-off main entrance' (GW Hatchet, Sept 21; ABC News; Al Jazeera Sept 19).

EVIDENCE - toward continued closure:
- Sept 15, 2026: Trump-appointed board voted (its second such vote) to close the center for two years of renovations; the board resolution indicates the building would not reopen until 2028 (CNN Sept 16; PBS NewsHour Sept 16).
- Sept 17, 2026 court declaration by Exec Director / COO Matt Floca: closure is due to 'acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration'; 'will last for seven days, unless extended'; he intends to 'reevaluate the need for continued closure on a weekly basis' (The Hill, Boston Globe, Denver Gazette, Sept 17). Cited a Sept 4 DC storm that dislodged ~1.5m of Grand Foyer ceiling plaster (no injuries) plus a roof terrace canopy inspection (Estadao Sept 20; CNN Sept 16).
- Apr 22, 2026 (CNN): Floca said the two-year closure plan was his own idea - the official who declared the temporary safety closure is the same official who authored the long closure plan.
- Sept 18, 2026: 14+ employees laid off, including the top spokesperson, board-relations head, and marketing/sales, IT and communications staff; third layoff round of 2026 after Mar 26 and Apr 10 (WaPo Sept 18).
- Aug 18, 2026: the National Symphony Orchestra announced its entire 2026-27 season at six other DMV venues (Lisner 24 concerts, Strathmore 13, Schlesinger 9, GMU 8, Clarice 2, Lincoln 2) - first season away from the Center since 1971. Its October programs (Oct 8-9/10 Noseda; Oct 22-23 Slatkin) are relocated, not cancelled. The board had not approved the NSO budget for the fiscal year beginning Oct 1, 2026 (Washington Classical Review, WTOP, WUSA9, Symphony.org).
- Washington National Opera withdrew its residence; a long 2025-26 run of artist cancellations (Hamilton, Renee Fleming, Philip Glass, SF Ballet, NYC Ballet, Martha Graham) plus falling ticket sales (NPR Jan 20, 2026; Rolling Stone; Wikipedia cancellations list).
- Trump publicly warned the center may not reopen unless his name can be affixed to the building, and was photographed Sept 16 aboard Air Force One with a placard reading 'Kennedy Center DEMOLISH[ED]' (CNN Sept 16). Sept 21 documents show Trump appointees planned to deaccession the art collection (ARTnews Sept 21).
- Judge Cooper's Sept 17 order 'does not require the building to reopen immediately' (Washington Times Sept 17); it requires 30 days' notice before demolition or major physical change and a Board status update by Sept 23.
- DOJ appealed the ruling barring Trump's name, and said it planned to appeal the order requiring the center stay open; per Cooper's schedule, defendants faced a Friday Sept 18 deadline to move to vacate and for summary judgment; discovery opened Sept 16 and closes Oct 9 (Forbes Sept 16; CNBC Sept 16).
- Under the separate two-year renovation plan, only the REACH was to stay partially open, with 'bare bones' staffing - and REACH-only access does not satisfy this question.

EVIDENCE - toward reopening:
- A standing preliminary injunction from May 29, 2026 blocked the proposed two-year closure and ordered the original name restored within 14 days; it bars implementing shutdown plans until the board approves a closure consistent with the ruling and the court lifts or modifies the injunction (Wikipedia; CNBC Sept 16). Reporting states that officially closing the monument 'would violate' that order.
- Floca's declaration says the closure covers 'certain parts' / 'most public spaces' with severe deterioration, and that he would try to open areas if they are found safe - a partial reopening is contemplated in his own filing. Government lawyers told the court the building 'could reopen in a week.'
- Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), ex officio trustee, filed Sept 16 for an emergency hearing, calling the closure 'unlawful' and 'a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently' and 'a recipe for Defendants extending their shutdown forever'; Cooper said he would 'schedule a prompt hearing if necessary' after reviewing the response, and ordered discovery into board demolition actions.
- Large public pressure: Sept 18 rally of hundreds to several thousand (ABC 'hundreds'; Art Newspaper ~1,500; organizers 2,500; one report 6,400+), organized by Hands Off the Arts against the sudden closure and the security fencing; Democratic legislators vocally opposed.
- Congress appropriated $257M in July 2025 for renovations, and reporting notes renovation work is being delayed pending judicial authorization - i.e., the physical work the closure is nominally for had not started as of Sept 20.
- Normal operations, when open, include free daily Millennium Stage programming, free tours, and long daily Grand Foyer public hours - so if any access resumes at all the building is routinely open to walk-in public.

calls.reasoning: Status quo at Now is a fenced, locked main building, closed since Sept 16 under a sworn 'seven days, unless extended' declaration with weekly reevaluation (checkpoints ~Sept 23 and ~Sept 30 before the window). Every actor controlling the doors prefers closure: board voted for a ~2-year shutdown, DOJ moved to dissolve the May 29 injunction, Trump tied reopening to the naming dispute, operations/marketing staff were laid off Sept 18, NSO and WNO relocated their full 2026-27 seasons, and the main-building calendar for Oct 2 is empty. YES requires either (a) Cooper reading the Sept 23 status report as pretext, ordering reopening, and that converting into physical public entry within nine days against a life-safety declaration and a probable stay request - he already declined emergency relief on Sept 16-17 and expressly did not require immediate reopening - or (b) a voluntary partial reopening of 'areas found safe.' I price (b) below the runs' 3-4%: the ~60-ft plaster collapse is in the Grand Foyer, the very space general visitation, tours and Millennium Stage occupy, so 'safe areas' plausibly means back-of-house, not public entry. Offsetting: the YES bar is very low (any public entry, any purpose, any moment), and contempt exposure gives a token-reopening incentive - that keeps this at 6% rather than 3%.
calls.reconciliation: Disputes were few because all three runs shared a skeleton. FACTUAL: (1) status of the DOJ motion to dissolve the May 29 injunction - Run 1 reports it filed Sept 19, Run 2 says intended-not-confirmed, Run 3 notes a court-set Sept 18 deadline to move to vacate; no web access this run, but the three are mutually compatible with a filing on/about Sept 18-19 and no run reports a ruling, so the uncertainty is carried rather than resolved and it does not change direction. (2) Renovation figure $285M vs the $257M appropriation - unsettled, immaterial to one day's physical access. (3) Market coverage - all three independently found no contract on public access or reopening; the Polymarket books are demolition-announcement contracts with different triggers and deadlines and $183-247 volume, Manifold's is demolition-by-2029; treated as evidence of general pessimism about the institution, not as an anchor, and not blended. JUDGMENT, unresolved by evidence: whether the May 29 injunction legally bars this closure - Beatty calls it pretext, DOJ says the order does not forbid a temporary closure, and Run 2's quotation of the injunction (it does not categorically prohibit a closure re-approved prudently) suggests the text is genuinely ambiguous; I take Cooper's own Sept 17 conduct - denying an emergency hearing, ordering a status report and discovery instead - as the best evidence of how he reads it, which favors NO. JUDGMENT where I depart from all three members rather than averaging: the voluntary 'open areas found safe' path, priced at 3-4% by Runs 1 and 3, should be lower, because the Sept 4 plaster collapse is located in the Grand Foyer - the principal general-visitation space - so partial reopening of structurally cleared areas does not naturally produce public entry into the resolving structure. That single evidentiary point, not a compromise, puts me one point below the pool at 0.06.
